item.title: Windows Server 2028 won't be compatible by default
item.description: Microsoft has pushed Windows Server 2028 into public preview, with an eye on beefed-up security, new infrastructure support, and the inevitable nod to AI. Neil Hinnant, a director on the Windows Server team, talked up the security tweaks. There's a hardened Server Core configuration by default and a new security baseline. "Trusted Launch extends protection to virtual machines," he wrote . "Confidential VM support begins a journey to support integrity-protected runtimes on supported CVM hardware." Server Core will therefore arrive locked down by default – good news for security, potentially less so for administrators whose existing configurations depend on more permissive settings. "For years, Windows Server shipped compatible by default," wrote Senior Product Manager Christina Curlette. "Making the server secure was up to you, usually by applying the Security Baseline or your own hardening scripts after setup." With Windows Server 2028 (and starting from Windows Server Insider Preview build 29706), Server Core will be installed hardened. "Hundreds of security settings are on from first boot," Curlette wrote. "Because the defaults are now locked down, some things that worked on Windows Server 2025 may not work on Windows Server 2028 without changes. This includes older protocols, legacy authentication, and some management tools and scripts." For a company obsessed with backward compatibility, this is quite the step. Welcome though the hardening is, administrators will need to test carefully: working on Windows Server 2025 won't guarantee a smooth ride in the brave new world. AI gets a role on both sides of the security fence: helping uncover vulnerabilities and giving Microsoft another reason to sell servers. Windows Server 2028 is being pitched for running models locally, with support for accelerators such as AMD's Instinct MI350P. Not every server is destined to babysit a model, however, and the storage changes may be more immediately useful to enterprise administrators. Windows Server 2028 will enable native NVMe storage by default, along with NVMe over TCP and RDMA. Booting from ReFS is also planned, adding another item to the storage upgrade list. Intune management for Windows Server has also entered preview. Azure Arc, with its cloud-native management workflows, is obviously still around, while Intune brings a more familiar management interface for administrators already using it for endpoints. Hinnant acknowledged that this was a "major release," and it looks like the security hardening alone will require a good deal of thought from administrators before organizations adopt the eventual production release. Esben Dochy, Principal Technical Evangelist for SecOps at Lansweeper, told The Register that Microsoft had indicated that the hardened security only applied to new installations. "If that remains in the final release," he said, "in-place upgrades could be easier. The catch is that those servers may also miss out on the new security defaul

item.title: India's SatLeo Labs wants to build a 'thermometer for Earth' in space
item.description:
Sharmila Kuthunur is an independent space journalist based in Bengaluru, India. Her work has also appeared in Scientific American, Science, Astronomy and Live Science, among other publications. She holds a master's degree in journalism from Northeastern University in Boston. 

AHMEDABAD, India — As climate disasters grow more frequent and severe, a young Indian space-tech startup is betting it can help the world act sooner by reading Earth's temperature from orbit in near-real time. SatLeo Labs, based here in western India, is building what it calls a " thermometer for Earth " in space. It plans to achieve its roadmap to deliver frequent, near-real-time thermal data through Pyro, a planned constellation of 15 microsatellites that will circle the planet in low Earth orbit by early 2030, if all goes to plan. Equipped with thermal sensors and onboard artificial intelligence , the satellites will measure the heat radiating from Earth's surface at a resolution finer than 10 meters (33 feet), which is sharp enough to map heat variations down to street level, the company says. "It's going to be that precise," SatLeo Labs co-founder Urmil Bakhai told Space.com in a recent interview. That level of detail, he said, helps distinguish temperatures across a single city and pinpoint urban hot spots, allowing governments and policymakers to plan targeted interventions and more heat-resilient city designs. The company is also targeting agriculture, and for good reason: Research suggests that thermal data can directly reveal water stress on crops days before leaves wilt, discolor or show other visible damage, unlike visible-light satellite imagery. Other uses the company is eyeing include spotting forest fires early, tracking industrial emissions and, on the defense side, detecting sudden temperature spikes from missile launches . Down the road, the team also envisions hyper-local uses. Near the top of its list are live heat maps built into navigation apps that could help gig-economy workers in India. These folks, who often ride motorcycles, could use the data to pick cooler routes during heat waves, said Bakhai. "We are in space, but we're solving problems on Earth ," said Shravan Bhati, SatLeo's co-founder and CEO. First, however, the company has to prove that its homegrown hardware works in space. On Oct. 1, SatLeo launched its first technology demonstrator, TAPAS-1, aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket as part of the Transporter-18 rideshare mission. Short for "Thermal Access Platform for Analytics & Solutions," TAPAS-1 is India's first commercial thermal payload in orbit and the first of SatLeo's three planned test payloads meant to validate its technology. Once complete, the 15-satellite Pyro fleet will scan all of the world's land surface at least twice a day, Bakhai said. item.title: Police arrest 15 over £1.5M 'we'll recover your losses' scam targeting elderly
item.description: Fifteen people have been arrested over an alleged scam that squeezed more money from investment fraud victims by offering to help recover their losses. City of London Police searched 17 London addresses on November 11 and apprehended 14 men and one woman. All have since been released on bail. Investigators say the suspected fraudsters posed as regulators to persuade previous victims that compensation was available. Reports submitted through the UK's Report Fraud service helped investigators trace the compensation pitch to around 3,000 recipients since October 2025. Most victims were elderly, police said. The offers arrived by letter and email, promising redress for earlier investment losses. City of London Police said the victims were initially targeted by a range of investment scams related to art, carbon credits, land, whisky, wine, and pensions, and that some took place more than a decade prior to their re-victimization. Targets were directed to a company that demanded a holding fee before supposedly reclaiming their money. Police say those who paid were left further out of pocket. "Today's action sends a clear message to those who target vulnerable people for financial gain: you will be pursued and will face robust action," said Nik Adams, deputy commissioner at the City of London Police. "Behind every fraud report is a real person whose trust has been damaged, and in some cases, whose life savings have been stolen. We know the impact of these crimes can be devastating. "This case highlights the importance of reporting fraud through the Report Fraud service. Information provided by victims helped investigators link reports together, uncover the wider conspiracy, and identify those involved. It is a powerful reminder that every report counts and can play a vital role in bringing offenders to justice." The investigation also extends beyond London, with police identifying locations linked to the case in Kent and Hertfordshire. The searches resulted in officers seizing cash, drugs, and other high-value items, including a watch worth around £230,000, with the total haul valued at more than £2 million. Police put losses identified so far at £1.5 million and expect that figure to rise as the investigation continues. Knowing the details of an earlier scam doesn't make a caller trustworthy, police warned. That information can be used to sell victims a second fraud. Report Fraud has also highlighted substantial losses in other scams affecting older people. Fraudsters exploiting positions of trust stole a reported £93.8 million during 2025/26. People aged 70 and over lost more than £51 million, with relatives, friends, carers, and others entrusted with their finances among the perpetrators. Report Fraud received 3,812 reports in this category. "The impact of fraud extends far beyond financial loss, especially when it is carried out by those who are trusted by the victim," said Mark Evans, president at the Law Society of England and Wales. item.title: Annoying Trump and dodging Flock: inside MapQuest’s contrarian comeback
item.description: After refusing to obey the president’s Lake Ontario order, MapQuest briefly rose to No 1 in navigation apps. It’s now a tool in the US anti-surveillance movement I am among the legion of former PC desk occupants with warm memories of MapQuest, the Y2K-era travel website that kept millennial drivers on course with sheaves of printed-out directions – a quantum leap over the ungainly glovebox map. But I assumed it had long since gone the way of AIM and Skype, its manual turn-by-turn guidance made obsolete by big tech. Proof of life came in January 2025, when Donald Trump issued an executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America – a change Apple Maps and Google Maps promptly adopted, while MapQuest … did nothing. Not only had it never signed off, MapQuest was reinventing itself as a plucky oppositional hero, the app most likely to uphold your geographical beliefs. Continue reading...

item.title: England should be 'proud' after ODI series win but 'work to do' for Australia
ULA says Vulcan lacked the oomph to get Amazon satellites to orbit
item.description: United Launch Alliance (ULA) says poor booster performance appears to have doomed Sunday's Vulcan mission, which lost an Amazon Leo satellite payload on the rocket's return to flight. ULA's initial assessment points to trouble almost immediately. "Early indications are that just after liftoff the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance," it said. As a result, stage separation occurred at too low an altitude, and the rocket was not traveling fast enough for the payload to reach orbit. The second stage appeared to perform well, with its RL10 engines operating as planned, but that wasn't enough to make up for the shortfall, and the mission failed . ULA lost telemetry approximately ten minutes into flight. An investigation is underway, led by ULA and overseen by the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), which had to activate two Debris Response Areas where debris was falling. The agency directs aircraft to leave these areas, and others are prevented from entering. Late Wednesday afternoon GMT, ULA posted an update stating that it looks like it might be the fuel supply rather than the BE-4 engines that caused the underperformance of the booster. The company wrote: “Preliminary indications are that the low booster thrust was the result of inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines." Previous flights had been blighted by problems with the solid rocket boosters , designed to give the rocket a kick at launch. Those issues prompted a stand-down while investigators examined the cause. This time, ULA said: "All indications are that the solid rocket booster performance was nominal, following nozzle improvements implemented for this launch." Attention therefore turns to Vulcan's liquid-fueled core stage, powered by two Blue Origin BE-4 engines, though that does not establish an engine fault. Fuel delivery or another first-stage system could also be responsible, and the investigation is ongoing. The BE-4 also powers Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket, which exploded on the launchpad during a ground test in May. In August, Blue Origin boss Dave Limp said that the issue originated at the main oxygen valve on one of the BE-4 engines. Modifications were made to deal with the problem. The upper stage's apparently normal performance may offer some reassurance to NASA, although the investigation remains at an early stage. The agency dropped the delayed Exploration Upper Stage earlier this year and is pursuing a stretched Centaur V alongside its existing interim cryogenic propulsion stage as options for Artemis IV. NASA is targeting Artemis IV for early 2028 and Artemis V for later that year. ULA said: "We truly understand the impact this has on our customers and are committed to returning to flight as safely and quickly as we can." item.title: 1 light-day from Earth! NASA's Voyager 1 probe hits huge milestone in interstellar space
item.description: null NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft is now one light-day from Earth — so far away that it takes signals a full 24 hours to reach the probe. Voyager 1 launched on Sept. 5, 1977, just a couple of weeks after Voyager 2 lifted off. But Voyager 1 launched on a faster trajectory than its twin and has just become the first spacecraft to ever reach one light-day away, which is equivalent to about 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers), or the distance that one light particle travels in 24 hours. The milestone — which Voyager 1 hit today (Nov. 18) at 5:16 a.m. EST (1016 GMT) — shows the incredible ingenuity, technical ability and creativity from the teams at NASA that continue to innovate to keep this mission going nearly five decades later. "The Earth and Voyager are exactly 24 hours apart at the speed of light," Voyager Project Scientist Linda Spilker told Space.com. "It's a very special moment where Voyager 1 is about 16.1 billion miles away, and we're celebrating that moment because it's the first human-made object to actually reach one light-day distance." All things Voyager The two Voyager spacecraft have been on one serious ride since launching in 1977. And each of these twin probes has taken a unique and historic journey through our solar system and beyond. On Voyager 1's trip through our cosmic neighborhood, for example, it made countless groundbreaking observations of planets and moons that we had never before seen up close (or at all). The probe discovered a ring around Jupiter as well as the planet's moons Thebe and Metis. It also found five new moons and a new ring around Saturn. "Voyager 1 flew past the Jupiter system and took images of Jupiter's moon Io, and it actually discovered that Io is volcanically active. So, images that were taken showed these volcanoes that were actively erupting, and we learned that Io is actually the most volcanically active body in our solar system, which is just amazing," Cynthia Phillips, a project scientist for NASA's Europa Clipper mission, told Space.com about one of Voyager 1's many discoveries. The Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 probes both flew past Jupiter in 1979, on their way out of the solar system. Represented here is Voyager 2's encounter with Jupiter. NASA/JPL A close-up of Jupiter's Great Red Spot as seen by one of NASA's Voyager spacecraft. NASA/JPL-Caltech Voyager 1 took photos of Jupiter and two of its satellites (Io, left, and Europa). The new study says that moons orbiting a gas giant planet greater than 8 Jupiter masses could help astronomers detect a rogue planet. NASA/JPL A mosaic of Jupiter by Voyager 1. JPL Jupiter and two of its moons — Io, to the left, and Europa — as seen by Voyager 1 on Feb. 13, 1979. JPL/NASA Voyager 1 image of Jupiter's volcanic moon Io, showing the active plume of a volcano called Loki. NASA/JPL/USGS "And then, as Voyager 1 continued out to the Saturn system, it actually discovered that Saturn's large moon Titan has a very thick atmosphere surrounding it," she adde

item.title: Beyoncé Becomes First Artist in Grammy History to Earn 100 Nominations!
item.description: Beyoncé becomes the first artist in history to reach 100 career Grammy nominations. Photo Credit: Beyoncé/Instagram If you have ever wondered what triple digits look like on music’s biggest stage, Beyoncé just gave everyone the answer. The Houston-born global music superstar has officially become the first artist in history to reach 100 career Grammy nominations, hitting the milestone with her latest nod for “ Morning Dew ( Donk )”, which is nominated for Best R&B Solo Performance at the 69th Annual Grammy Awards (2027 Grammys). Released in July 2026 ahead of the 20th anniversary of her sophomore album B’Day, “Morning Dew (Donk)” puts her in a category alongside Kehlani , Victoria Monét , Jill Scott , and Nigerian star Tems . To put the 100-nomination milestone into perspective, no other recording artist has ever crossed into triple digits since the Grammys began. Beyoncé had previously been tied with her husband, Jay-Z , at 88 nominations each before breaking that tie in 2024 with 11 nods for Cowboy Carter to reach 99—and this latest recognition pushes her even further ahead as the artist with the highest number of Grammy nominations in history. Beyoncé holding her three Grammy trophies at the 67th Annual Grammy Awards in 2025. Photo Credit: Beyoncé/Instagram It is also a good reminder of how long she has been doing this at the highest level. Beyoncé’s Grammy journey started all the way back in 2000 as part of Destiny’s Child with “Bills, Bills, Bills”, and across more than two decades as a solo artist, group member, and collaborator, she has built a record that keeps stretching further ahead of the pack. Alongside holding the title for the most Grammy nominations of all time, she is already the most awarded artist in Grammy history with 35 wins, a record she first broke in 2023 when she surpassed late conductor Georg Solti ’s 31 trophies. She pushed that tally even higher at the 2025 Grammys, taking home three awards—Album of the Year and Best Country Album for Cowboy Carter, as well as Best Country Duo/Group Performance for “II Most Wanted” alongside Miley Cyrus . Now all eyes turn to Sunday, 7 February 2027, when the 2027 Grammy Awards take place at the Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles and we find out whether nomination number 100 turns into Grammy win number 36. item.title: UK.gov JV gets £178M Home Office hosting deal. Without competition
item.description: The Home Office has awarded a contract worth £178 million to a public-private hosting services joint venture - without competition - to support critical national infrastructure. According to a notice published last week , Crown Hosting Data Centres (CHDC) won the seven-year contract to support "essential national infrastructure underpinning the Home Office's most critical systems, including border security, the Police National Computer (PNC), and core intelligence environments." CHDC is a joint venture between the Cabinet Office, which owns 25 percent, and Ark Data Centres Ltd, which owns the rest. It was set up in 2015 for the express purpose of providing hosting services for the government. The award was made through an existing framework agreement, set up in February 2022, awarded to CHDC without competition via a Voluntary Ex-Ante Transparency Notice . The service is set to support Critical National Infrastructure, although the notice does not reveal specific services requested. Mention of continued support for the Police National Computer may raise eyebrows. The Home Office is managing the transition of the aging legacy system to the Law Enforcement Data Service (LEDS) under the National Law Enforcement Data Program (NLEDP). A notice in December 2024 said that the Home Office was "focused on the development and adoption of LEDS products to replace existing PNC capability across all police forces and other non-policing PNC consumers, enabling the retirement by March 2026 (the point at which PNC support will expire)." The government had previously set a target of decommissioning the PNC in 2022. The Register has asked the Home Office to clarify why Crown Hosting support is necessary beyond this date. The PNC – which is based on mainframe technology dating from the 1970s – was at the center of a scandal in 2021 when a technology failure led to the loss of 413,000 records of evidence . The incident, which left then Prime Minister Boris Johnson floundering in Parliament, was the result of a scripting error in code designed to weed out records to be deleted from the PNC, a system running on a Fujitsu BS2000/OSD SE700-30 mainframe-based at a datacenter in Hendon, London. In 2022, the Cabinet Office awarded a contract worth up to £250 million to CHDC, also without outside competition. ®

item.title: SAP opens AI to on-prem customers, but cloud commitments could shut smaller firms out
item.description: SAP's commercial terms could put its latest AI tools out of reach for many customers, particularly smaller businesses running a single ERP system, the new chair of its German-speaking user group has warned. Thomas Henzler, appointed chair of DSAG last month, told The Register that Joule Studio 2.0 – SAP's upgraded platform for developing and deploying AI agents to automate business tasks – is a leap forward. Yet DSAG, which represents SAP users in Germany, Switzerland, and Austria, remains in talks with the vendor about the commercial conditions attached to access. In July 2023, CEO Christian Klein told investors that SAP's "newest innovations and capabilities" will only be delivered in the public or private cloud using RISE with SAP, the vendor's lift-shift-and-transform program launched with partners and cloud providers in early 2021. Customers running ERP software on-premises, or hosting it with a hyperscaler outside RISE, will miss out, he said. However, in May this year, SAP appeared to perform a U-turn . It said on-premises customers could access Joule 2.0 if they commit to a cloud "journey" through RISE with SAP, changing their support and commercial arrangements while migration projects are still underway. Henzler told The Reg : "There is a gap between the customer's reality and SAP's strategy for the autonomous enterprise. A lot of customers are still planning to migrate to S/4HANA, and now the question is, 'what do we have to do to use SAP AI, and what does it mean regarding the cloud strategy?' "Now it's a completely new strategy, a new approach, and a new underlying technology. The question is, what does it mean for existing projects, S/4HANA migrations, cloud migrations and so on? Is it necessary to rethink all the projects? Is there a big shift in the technology and architectures?" The DSAG chair said the biggest challenge in connecting legacy on-prem systems, such as ECC, to the new Joule suite is the commercial model. "Access requires a substantial RISE commitment and a minimum cloud-to-on-premise maintenance ratio. In practice, this creates a problem for customers with only one ECC system. To meet the cloud threshold, they have to convert their entire on-premises maintenance into a cloud subscription, which defeats the purpose of an on-premises connector. Consequently, the model only works for large enterprises with multiple SAP ERP systems that can, for example, migrate one system after the other to unlock AI for the rest," he said. "In the end, to get the benefit you have to start a RISE with SAP migration. Therefore, the connector doesn't make sense for the majority of SME customers. From my perspective, this approach works only for large customers with multiple ERP systems, for example, if they take one system, move it to the cloud, and then another one. Then they can use AI, because they reach the needed ratio to use the on-prem connector. That is more or less a commercial approach. We need a solution for all customers, inde

item.description: Newlyweds Efya and Tomi Thomas at their white wedding reception in Accra. Photo Credit: Thret Studio/Instagram Two music stars, two countries, one beautiful love story! Nigerian singer Tomi Thomas and Ghanaian songstress Efya have made things official, celebrating their union in Accra with a wedding that brought Nigerian and Ghanaian traditions together. From their coordinated traditional looks to their elegant white wedding outfits and a song Tomi made especially for his bride, there was plenty to love about this celebration. item.title: UK MPs want AI watchdog with power to pull the plug on dangerous models
item.description: UK MPs want a watchdog with the power to pull the plug on dangerous AI models, rather than leave the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic to decide when they've gone too far. In a report shared with The Register ahead of publication on Wednesday, a parliamentary committee is calling for an AI Safety and Security Bill that would give a watchdog powers to intervene while models are still being developed. It could halt high-risk training and testing, block deployments, or suspend AI services if the risks can't be contained. LLMs are trained on billions of learned parameters and so developers can't always predict what a model will do in every situation. The recommendations come from Parliament's Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee, which questioned researchers, former AI employees, and representatives from OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Anthropic, and Meta. All four companies assured MPs they wouldn't release models they considered unsafe. The trouble is, they don't use the same yardstick for safety, and UK law doesn't generally require them to get an independent opinion before releasing anything. "We cannot give today’s AI leaders unfettered freedom to behave like modern-day Dr Frankensteins, creating dangers beyond anyone’s control," said committee chair Liam Byrne MP. Just as with aviation, pharma or nuclear safety, UK government want to rely on manufacturers' assurance alone, and want regulation. "Our hearings exposed gaps in independent scrutiny, incident reporting and powers to stop unsafe systems. Once some models are released, they cannot reliably be recalled," added Byrne. "Protection must begin while systems are being built and tested." The committee's report, Guardrails for Growth: Making AI Safe, identifies ten holes in Britain's approach to AI safety, including the lack of mandatory incident reporting, limited access for independent testers, and inadequate protections for whistleblowers. The UK already has an AI Security Institute (AISI), which has made a name for itself testing some of the world's most powerful models, but its work depends on voluntary cooperation, and it has no authority to stop a company releasing a model that raises safety concerns. MPs want AISI to continue its testing work while a separate regulator takes responsibility for enforcement. Developers of designated high-risk systems would have to provide evidence supporting their safety claims and give independent researchers access to examine them. Significant changes to a model's capabilities or safeguards would trigger further scrutiny. Former AI employees also told MPs that raising safety concerns can come at a price. Restrictive contracts, commercial pressures, and financial disincentives can all discourage staff from speaking out, the committee heard. MPs want stronger legal protections for whistleblowers and compulsory reporting of AI incidents and near misses. There's a fair bit of money riding on this, too. item.title: Tochukwu Ekoh: What My Friend’s Passing Taught Me About Kindness
item.description: A thoughtful young woman sits in a relaxed pose in a serene bedroom, reflecting peacefully. Photo credit: Alex Green/Pexels. I lost someone recently, and since then, I have found myself revisiting little moments, conversations and encounters I probably would not have given much thought to otherwise. We weren’t particularly close , or I wouldn’t describe our relationship that way . We had reconnected after a long time and started seeing each other more often, especially after I resumed work following an accident I was involved in. He gradually became part of my daily routine. Whenever I went to work, he would come to pick me up from the office, and we would go home together. In many ways, he looked out for me and made sure I got home safely. We started talking more. We would discuss life, share experiences and occasionally open up about things happening in our individual lives. There was also an emotional dimension to our friendship. He was interested in me romantically, I realised, but I didn’t feel the same way. I tried to understand my feelings, but the truth was that I simply wasn’t in love with him. I couldn’t manufacture feelings that weren’t there. Then I heard that he passed away. My first reaction, strangely, was guilt. I began asking myself: Was I a good friend to him? Was I kind enough? Was I considerate? Did I treat him well? Could I have done something differently? I caught myself wondering whether I should have given him a chance . Perhaps I should have allowed him to love me. But then would I have done that out of genuine affection or simply out of pity? And would that have been fair to either of us? My understanding is that not returning someone’s romantic feelings does not mean we cannot offer them genuine friendship, kindness and compassion. I didn’t owe him romantic love, but I could have been a good friend. That has stayed with me. Beyond the guilt, there was another question I couldn’t get out of my head: Why did God allow us to reconnect? Why, after such a long time, did our paths have to cross again? Why did we have to start talking, sharing experiences and becoming familiar with each other again, only for him to die shortly afterwards? Why him? Why at that particular time? What was the reason for that reconnection, and why did it have to end this way? The timing of certain events leaves you with more questions than answers. What makes this loss even more difficult to comprehend is how it happened. I had been the one who suffered an accident, yet I survived and was gradually recovering. He wasn’t sick. He hadn’t been involved in an accident. He simply slipped and fell, sustained an injury, and bled out. His body was not discovered until three days later. Three days. The loneliness he must have experienced within those three days, the possibility that he needed someone, and the heartbreaking thought that nobody knew what had happened to him. I cannot fully comprehend it. It also made me confront something I had perhaps never

item.title: Time for frustrated M365 customers to stage a 'distributed denial of satisfaction' action
item.description: I briefly helped with Microsoft Australia’s PR efforts in the early 2000s, when IE 6 and Windows were so bug-prone they essentially represented a welcome mat for hackers and required a deluge of patches admins couldn’t handle. Microsoft responded to that mess with a message about security being a shared responsibility involving people, process, and technology. A quarter of a century later, Microsoft’s business practices still make its customers reluctantly share the cost of its failings – most recently last week’s massive M365 outage. To protest that mess, Microsoft customers should create a new cloudy meltdown – on the pages the software giant uses to process applications for compensation after it fails to meet service level agreements. Yes, you read that right: “applications.” When Microsoft experiences an outage, customers must apply to get the service credits they’re entitled by finding the “Outage ID” related to each incident. The application page is buried deep in the Microsoft 365 Admin Center and the Outage ID is recorded elsewhere. Microsoft appears not to offer a facility for bulk uploads, so the channel partners who manage so many M365 implementations have extra work to do. That’s outrageous because the implicit promise of the cloud is that it delivers more value for less effort. Yet Microsoft requires users to do extra work to seek redress for its mistakes. Cloud also delivers fat profits for investors. Which is probably why Microsoft, which can clearly bill its customers regularly and reliably and therefore knows which services they use, hasn’t done the work to link its uptime meters and billing systems so it can automate crediting customers after outages. I understand Microsoft thinks AI is quite good at that sort of integration. Maybe its enormously reduced workforce will need it to get the job done. But rather than vibe-coding its way out of this, decency demands Microsoft quickly decide that all users impacted by last week’s automatically receive service credits, rather than asking them apply for their entitlements. If Microsoft doesn’t get proactive, the magnitude of this outage represents a moment in which its customers can show the software giant it must do better – perhaps by filing so many applications for credit that managers who oversee Redmond’s systems and finances can’t help but notice a spike of activity. Thinks of this as a distributed denial of satisfaction attack signaling that Microsoft can't solve this particular outage with a glib apology and a blog post. ®

item.title: A Chinese bottle-cap manufacturer brilliantly deflated AI hype
item.description: Shanghai is one of the world’s largest and busiest cities but is surprisingly quiet . Electric automobiles cruise silently, chased by hushed flocks of electric scooters. When I visited in early November to attend the local edition of the AI Engineer conference, I found China's attitude to AI is also quite relaxed. That's not to say interest in the topic is low, but I didn't perceive any anxious artificial-general-intelligence-is-coming-and-will-destroy-us vibe. The only conference talk that referenced AGI came from Ying Yang, a neuroscience PhD and serious influencer who has over 3.4 million followers on Chinese micro-blogging service Weibo , who enthused about the marketing and product development opportunities opening up to those who prepare for what’s coming. AGI isn't P(doom) for the Chinese AI practitioners I met; it's a great new marketing tool. Some of this may be due to the fact that the major US model makers like OpenAI, Anthropic and Google are effectively inaccessible on the Chinese side of the Great Firewall. Engineers in China use DeepSeek or Kimi or GLM or MiniMax or MiMo or Qwen, all of which are now more than good enough for almost any task, and all offered without reference to The Terminator . That's not to say that Chinese engineers and designers aren't facing the same crisis of self-worth we've seen elsewhere. A spectacular keynote from Ryo Lu asked, "When we can do anything, do we still know what we want?" Are our measures of self-worth pointless when we can no longer prove who we are by how many lines of code we've written, or frameworks we've designed? Ryo landed on a line I'm hearing more frequently: "I want to build tools to help me be more and more involved, not prove that I'm needed less and less." What followed showed just how good that tooling has become and what an AI engineer can do with it. I saw an impressive demo from AutoArk of a 35 billion-parameter model running in just 2.5GB of smartphone RAM on an iPhone 16 Pro. DYNA 's Zhong Shen showed how it builds robot hardware that will work with AI models updating every month. My favorite presentation came from a bottle cap manufacturer called named Zhu Shihui, who reminded everyone in the audience that “the last mile is half the journey.” Zhu flayed the class of consultants who never realize some manufacturing equipment is pre-digital but still insist every process can be easily automated. Never mind that workers in those factories lack deep digital skills (Zhu's average employee is in their late 40s) and that companies of this sort operate on margins so thin that resources simply aren't available to mount a complete transformation. Instead of swinging in on an AI wrecking ball, Zhu suggested the best approach is to exercise humility by seeking out an organization's tacit knowledge and using that as the basis for transformation. item.title: Temu's compliance regime is low-quality, fits badly, and full of holes, says Europe
item.description: Chinese e-tailer Temu has a reputation for selling low-quality knockoff products at low prices made possible through use of forced labor. Now, the European Commission has made a preliminary finding that the company also runs a low-quality compliance regime that means it’s not meeting its regulatory obligations. The Commission issued that finding yesterday, accusing Temu of breaching its Digital Services Act (DSA) obligation to operate serious measures that mitigate the risk of illegal products being offered on its platform. Temu is a marketplace that allows third parties to sell on its platform, a model that doesn’t relieve it of responsibility for the goods available on its site and apps. Eurocrats therefore have beef with Temu over several matters, including: Requiring sellers who use the platform to test the quality of “only a very small share of products,” and then often not bothering to check the reports; Not doing enough to prioritize checks of products in known high risk categories, like toys and cosmetics, then not following up on those checks; Running a moderation system that mostly considers whether products comply with Temu’s terms and conditions, rather than product safety; Not hiring enough human moderators to keep pace with growth in listings on Temu; When it finds stores selling non-compliant goods, Temu acts against that store – but not the trader who may sell the same products in multiple stores; Allowing stores to commit many serious infringements, including selling products that fail safety checks, before suspending their stores. A Temu spokesperson told The Register the company respectfully disagrees with the EC's findings. "Temu invests significantly in compliance infrastructure and human expertise and implements a suite of control measures that effectively mitigate illegal product risks with a consistently low incidence of problematic products," the spokesperson said. "We will review and respond to the preliminary findings carefully and will continue to engage constructively with the Commission. We are confident that we will reach an amicable resolution of the matter that fully addresses the Commission's remaining concerns." The EC has already tangled with Temu. In 2024 Eurocrats investigated its risk assessment processes. In May 2026, Eurocrats found Temu’s processes inadequate and levied a €200 million fine. Brussels also sent a €550 million fine to another Chinese e-tailer, Alibaba, for not doing enough to stop the sale of dangerous goods. This announcement of new action against Temu invoked Article 35 of the Digital Services Act, the sweeping regulation of online businesses under which the EU could fine Temu up to six percent of its global revenue and order corrective actions. Europe is concerned that the low prices Chinese e-tailers charge are enabled by forced labor and ignoring dangerous products. item.title: Oracle reveals fix-this-ASAP-grade Java4Shell bug that allows attacks on many third-party apps
item.description: The United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has urged Java users to immediately patch a high-severity flaw in the software, which attackers can use to crash the Java virtual machine or achieve unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE). Oracle revealed the flaw in its monthly patch dump for November , which offers 655 patches, 62 of them rated critical, affecting 62 products. Several of the flaws are rated more dangerous than the Java problem, CVE-2026-114938 , which Big Red didn’t single out as worthy of special attention despite CISA’s warning . The cyber-agency’s decision seems apt because vulnerability research and red teaming outfit Calif.io, which discovered the flaw, used its X account to claim news of the problem had leaked before public disclosure and the release of Oracle's fixes. By then, Calif had already tested the flaw, which it named “Java4Shell,” and found applications including Keycloak, Atlassian’s Jira and Confluence, Jenkins, Apache Kafka Broker, and Elasticsearch are susceptible to RCE. Calif, which also helped to find the PHP2Shell flaw , says the flaw is a memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder. “Base64 is a very common way of representing binary data as text. It is used in authentication protocols, to encode file uploads, and to deliver network messages,” the company explained. “To decode Base64 faster, OpenJDK uses specialized x86-64 CPU instructions to process many bytes at once.” “We discovered a bug in that optimized machine-level code that lets malformed input overwrite neighboring memory. With careful exploitation, the corruption can reveal sensitive memory, as Heartbleed did, or lead to remote code execution. The corruption itself can be triggered by just 64 A characters followed by a single =:” Calif applied the CVSS 4.0 bug-rating scheme and gave the flaw a critical-rated score of 9.2/10. Infosec outfit SentinelOne’s analysis suggests the flaw “sits in the Java standard library, so exploit traffic is specific to each application.” “Any Base64 value an application passes to java.util.Base64.Decoder can carry the payload, including HTTP Basic credentials, SAML artifacts, CSRF tokens, and MIME encoded words. In default configurations of the affected applications listed above, attackers can reach this code path prior to authentication.” Cisco’s Talos security team pointed out that the flaw is present in OpenJDK Java versions 17.0.6 and later running on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI (Vector Byte Manipulation Instructions) support enabled. “These vulnerabilities have already been tested against a suite of Java applications with success, but the attack surface is likely much larger as additional targets are tested and confirmed,” Talos advised. Cisco’s infosec experts urged adoption of the fixed versions of Java Oracle posted on Tuesday but noted it is possible to mitigate the flaw on x86-64 machines by starting the JVM with support for AVX-512 disabled. item.title: Daily disruptive outages that ground planes and halt work – welcome to the new normal
item.description: Another day, another disruptive network outage (or two) as government officials and company execs scramble to assure an anxious populace that these are not coordinated cyberattacks – and security experts call this the new normal. A classified network that the US National Security Agency uses for internal communications, called NSANet, went offline on Tuesday in what the agency described as a “temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance.” “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues,” the NSA said in a statement following media reports about the outage. “NSA's infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.” Around the same time, Apple users began reporting issues across multiple services – including Apple Support, iCloud, the App Store, Apple Pay, and more – with Apple retail stores worldwide also reportedly experiencing disruptions that halted sales and in-person support. A day earlier, customers at major US banks including JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, and US Bank reported service outages that Chase attributed to “a software bug in on-premise hardware systems - there is no evidence this is cyber-related.” All of these high-profile outages followed last week’s US Federal Aviation Authority (FAA) order g rounding all planes on Friday due to problems with copper wiring during an L3Harris network upgrade, and a Microsoft 365 outage on Thursday. Redmond later blamed the massive service disruption on a faulty software update it pushed back in July. Despite the weekend respite from network outages, your humble vulture still had to field is-this-the-beginning-of-the-end questions from friends and family all day Saturday and Sunday, most of whom suspected Russia or China – maybe even Iran – caused the spate of downed systems and services. A highly sophisticated, coordinated nation-state hack would be a much more exciting cause for the disruptions. The real culprit, however, appears to be aging, under-funded infrastructure , riddled with decades-old bugs and held together by digital sticks and glue . “As someone who started out as a hacker , I know how tempting it is to connect the dots when major systems fail one after another,” Remedio CEO Tal Kollender told The Register, adding that there’s “no credible public evidence that these outages were part of a coordinated cyberattack,” and most have been attributed to technical failures. “What concerns me more is what these incidents reveal about the fragility of our digital infrastructure. We've built an interconnected world on layers of aging systems, complex configurations, and dependencies that organizations don't always fully understand. A single misconfiguration, failed update, or broken dependency can create disruption on a massive scale, even without an attacker,” Kollender said. “The uncomfor

item.title: GPU giants throw HPC users some tasty crumbs
item.description: At Supercomputing 2026 this week, Nvidia unveiled a new variant of its Rubin GPUs aimed at – you’ll never believe it – high performance computing (HPC). The creatively named Rubin HPC promises more than 50,000 CUDA cores, nearly twice that of the AI-focused version of the chip that Nvidia unveiled earlier this year. It will arrive sometime in 2028. According to Dan Ernst, Nvidia’s senior director of supercomputing, the new chip offers a rebalanced architecture optimized for the kinds of simulation, engineering, and high-performance analytics workloads common in the HPC and scientific computing communities. This is not the first time Nvidia has introduced specialized hardware. Last year, the company optimized its B300 accelerator for AI inferencing workloads. “Rubin HPC is the same idea,” Ernst told El Reg . “Within the Rubin platform, but we’re building variants to really focus on a specific sub domain of applications.” Details remain remarkably thin. Nvidia hasn’t disclosed peak performance memory capacity or bandwidth. That said, the chip will likely include features which show Nvidia can think beyond AI and still cares about the HPC community. Fearing that Nvidia could ignore HPC is reasonable becuase beginning with the launch of Blackwell Ultra (B300/GB300), the company traded double-precision matrix acceleration for higher throughput at lower-precisions. The result was a chip that at FP4 churned out 15 petaFLOPS of AI compute, but just 1.3 teraFLOPS at FP64. That's good for AI, but less useful for scientists. When Nvidia unveiled Rubin, it seemed the GPU-slinger would continue this trend. At 33 teraFLOPS, the chip was not only slower at FP64 than the Blackwell GPUs it replaced, but slower than Nvidia’s now four-year-old Hopper accelerators as well. Nvidia contended that for sparse vector-heavy workloads measured by the High Performance Conjugate Gradients (HPCG) benchmark, the higher ratio of memory bandwidth to compute should deliver meaningful performance gains. Meanwhile, for dense matrix-heavy workloads, for which benchmarks like High-Performance Linpack (HPL) are representative, Nvidia adopted a new strategy: FP64 emulation. We discussed the pros and cons of this technique in greater detail earlier this year, but in a nutshell it uses an algorithm derived from the so-called Ozaki Scheme. The algorithm works by decomposing FP64 matrix operations into a string of INT8 operations that, when run on Nvidia’s tensor cores, achieve higher-than-native performance. Nvidia, we’re told, isn’t using INT8, but it is unlocking substantial performance gains, at least for certain workloads. According to Nvidia, Rubin can churn out up to 200 emulated FP64 matrix teraFLOPS. While Ernst didn’t offer any specifics, he assured us that Nvidia’s HPC hardware should offer native FP64 matrix performance and customers won't have to rely entirely on emulation. item.title: NASA's Voyager 1 launched second, so how did it beat Voyager 2 to a light-day by nearly a decade?
item.description: null Voyager 1 is about to reach a light-day of distance in space, but Voyager 2 won't hit the mark until about 2035. Why the big difference? On Nov. 18, Voyager 1 will be so far away from Earth that it will take a full light-day (24 hours) to send a signal to the distant spacecraft, at 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). Since light is essentially the maximum speed in the universe (absent using devices like wormholes, or quantum-physics puzzles), it's a big deal — so big that NASA will be celebrating the milestone by asking fans to shine Morse Code signals at the sky. But why will Voyager 2 take nearly a decade longer? It comes down to choices made for speed and science during the twin missions' nearly 50-year journey, specifically during the first bit when they were flying by planets. The result is Voyager 1 is zooming out at a speed of 3.5 Earth-sun distances (astronomical units a year), while Voyager 2 has a more stately speed of 3.1 Earth-sun distances, according to NASA . Need for speed The original aim of both the spacecraft, which launched about two weeks apart in 1977 with Voyager 2 going first, was to look at Jupiter and Saturn. If funding persisted, which it did, the hope was to bring Voyager 2 past Uranus and Neptune, taking advantage of a rare planetary alignment. Voyager 1, by contrast, made a turn at Saturn to look at the planet's rings and the prebiotic (pre-life-chemistry) moon of Titan , before flying outside the plane of the solar system. NASA had a range of trajectory options to consider when launching the spacecraft, and elected to bring Voyager 1 at a faster trajectory — as illustrated in this video by Britannica, where you can quickly see the spacecraft overtaking Voyager 2 on its way to Jupiter even though Voyager 1. Voyager 1 arrived at Jupiter on March 5, 1979 while Voyager 2 got there four months later on July 9. The trajectories of Voyager 1 and 2 through the outer solar system. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) Each of the spacecraft then performed a "gravity assist"—a sort of slingshot around the planet in which they took a tiny bit of momentum from Jupiter to gain speed as the spacecraft flew to Saturn. This technique is used constantly, such as recently when the ESCAPADE Mars mission flew two spacecraft by Earth on the way to the Red Planet, as it allows spacecraft to gain speed while saving on fuel. The planets themselves don't slow down that much. "Because the planet is so much more massive than the spacecraft, the transfer doesn't affect the planet to any measurable extent, but to the spacecraft it's a big deal," the Planetary Society wrote . "For example, we can calculate that during the Voyager encounters with Jupiter in 1979, Jupiter slowed down by roughly 10 to the -24th power kilometers per second — a change much too small to measure." "But each Voyager gained about 10 km/s [6.2 miles/s], a pretty big number," the society continued about the Jupiter encounter. This was "enough to put them on a

item.title: Satya sorry for SaaS-y SNAFU - look over there, more AI!
item.description: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella's Ignite conference keynote on Tuesday was all about trust. He opened by promising to earn back trust after last week's massive M365 outage and went on to focus on the need for organizations to trust their AI models. "So last week in some sense was really a reminder of how critical digital infrastructure is as the dial tone for the world," said Nadella. "We know the trust you place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. And in that context, I know we have work to do to provide that resilience that you can count on, the world can count on, and we are committed to ensuring that we learn and we continuously improve." Speaking at San Francisco's Moscone Center, Nadella described three areas of focus for the company as it works to build what he referred to as a frontier ecosystem: "Keeping the human at the center of it all, ensuring that you have ownership over your organization's intelligence and learning, and trust." Anthrocentrism is a tough sell just weeks after offering buyouts to 60,000 employees . Describing the shift from hand-written code to agent-written code, Nadella suggested developers have moved from building software artifacts to building software factories that build those artifacts. "The important thing here though is to remember still that that human intent, that judgment, that experience, skills, expertise all very much matter," he said. People may judge development work, but ask them whether they have the same sense of ownership as when they wrote every line. As to ensuring that organizations have ownership over their intelligence, that borders on heresy for a company with massive cloud computing commitments specifically to run AI workloads. If everyone really owned their machine learning models and ran them in their own data centers and on employee computers, Azure would be in trouble. Yet Nadella emphasized ownership – which isn't at all obvious given the legal ambiguity of who owns AI generated code and whether it can be copyrighted . "In the age of AI, the key question is how do individual firms continually build and own their learning and tacit knowledge?" he said. "For an economy to remain an economy where many firms exist and thrive, intelligence by definition needs to be broadly distributed versus just collapsed into a couple of models." Suffice to say that Nadella is promoting client control over AI data that's processed mostly on equipment rented from Microsoft, with some allowance for customer-controlled infrastructure. But that still ought to concern frontier AI labs like Anthropic and OpenAI that favor a white-glove, black-box service model where they are the arbiters of access. As for the third pillar of Nadella's vision, that's trust, which remains missing in action. "How can you even trust all this powerful technology?" Nadella asked. item.title: Space is filling up with junk. Could laser-reflecting mirrors help humanity clean things up?
item.description: null A British startup thinks it can help humanity deal with its space junk problem. Millions of pieces of space debris circle Earth at the moment, according to the European Space Agency (ESA). Even the smallest fragments are potentially dangerous, given how fast stuff travels in orbit. Experts have proposed a range of measures to deal with this junk. The smallest bits, for example, may require big space nets, or lasering the stuff down to Earth. Large satellites are increasingly being deliberately deorbited these days, and a few have even been refueled to keep them operating in orbit — something that will likely start happening more and more over the coming years. Now, the British startup Foundational has another idea to throw into the mix: retroreflectors. The company argues that its tech can help fight the space-junk problem — and it just proved out a demo version in an orbital test. London-based Foundational recently tested its Retro-2 laser retroreflector system, which it developed in collaboration with ESA. The early-stage test was designed to ensure that Foundational's retroreflectors can return laser-ranging signals from a satellite , at altitudes between about 600 kilometers and 870 kilometers (about 370 to 540 miles), with a usable range distance of 300 to 1,400 km (186 to 870 miles). The long-term aim is to create a sort of tracking device for spacecraft, so they can be monitored in orbit even after they fall silent. Foundational's Retro-2 retroreflector, which is designed to help trackers keep tabs on satellites in orbit. It recently passed its first in-space test. (Image credit: Foundational) The tech, Foundational said in a statement today (Nov. 17), needs "no electronics, power or commands from its host spacecraft" and allows ground stations to keep tabs on the orbiting spacecraft. The demo mission launched this past July on SpaceX's Transporter-17 rideshare flight. It attached Retro-2 — a mini device with seven reflectors — to a small satellite that was integrated into an ION carrier craft operated by the Italian company D-Orbit. Retro-2 worked as advertised, successfully returning 6,111 laser shots beamed from the from the ground across five passes in low Earth orbit . "Our tests have shown that a device weighing just 50 grams [1.8 ounces] can deliver millimeter-level ranging precision," Dave Gooding, Foundational's co-founder and chief technical officer, said in today's statement. "As space becomes increasingly crowded, keeping satellites trackable throughout their lifetime and beyond is critical to managing collision risks." Foundational's Retro-2 retroreflector is seen before its July 2026 launch. The device is attached to its cubesat, which itself is integrated into one of D-Orbit's ION carrier craft. (Image credit: Foundational) Foundational is in its early stages — it was founded in 2025 and just emerged from stealth last month. item.title: 'Neuromancer:' Release date, cast & everything we know about Apple TV's new cyberpunk series
item.description: null We're in a bit of a cyberpunk revival at the moment. 2026 gave the excellent second season of Netflix’s "Cyberpunk: Edgerunners," and Prime Video's " Blade Runner 2099 " is just around the corner. 2027 will continue this trend with " Neuromancer " blasting onto Apple TV. Based on cyberspace guru William Gibson’s seminal 1984 novel, "Neuromancer" follows Case, a brilliant hacker who falls into a web of digital espionage and crime as he attempts an impossible corporate heist. The pulp noir novel has been hailed as a generational revelation, and its slang and terminology have become ingrained in computer nerd subcultures. After decades of development hell and failed attempts at various studios, "Neuromancer" and its plugged-in digital dystopia are finally jacking into the small screen in January 2027. Apple TV is already the secret home of amazing sci-fi, and "Neuromancer" will join the streamer's impressive roster of science fiction stalwarts like "Foundation", "Silo", "Invasion", "Dark Matter", "Murderbot", "For All Mankind", "Pluribus", and "Star City." Can it live up to the hype? We won't have to wait long for an answer. In the meantime, let's jack into cyberspace and scour the code for everything we know about Apple TV's "Neuromancer!" When is "Neuromancer"'s release date? Apple TV's "Neuromancer" fires up on January 22, 2027. (Image credit: Apple TV) Apple TV+’s Neuromancer officially powers up on Jan 22, 2027. It was first announced to be in full production back on July 1, 2025, which actually coincided with the 41st anniversary of the publication of William Gibson's absorbing book. Filming took place in Tokyo, Los Angeles, Istanbul, Canada, and London to create a truly international flair to replicate the novel’s action. Good news: NordVPN can help you get around those pesky geo-blocking restrictions so you can watch the streaming service you've paid for anywhere in the world. VIEW DEAL ON What is the plot of "Neuromancer"? (Image credit: Apple TV) Gibson's "Neuromancer" is a dense, jargon-heavy juggernaut of a book that demands intense concentration to absorb all the slang, lingo, computer terms, and staccato literary rhythms, but it's a fantastic immersion into a fully fleshed-out world. It's also worryingly prophetic, showing a world not unlike ours today in 2026. item.title: Astronomers discover rare black holes that formed when stars failed to go supernova
item.description: null Gravitational waves have revealed a population of black holes that may have been born when masssive stars failed to go supernova. Most of us know the origin story of black holes , or we thought we did. Massive stars run out of the fuel for nuclear fusion and their cores collapse. As this happens, the stars' outer layers expand outwards. Shockwaves from the core collapse strike the outer layers, triggering a supernova explosion. The collapsed core creates a black hole. However, new research based on gravitational wave data collected by LIGO (Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory) and its gravitational wave detector partners, Virgo and KAGRA (Kamioka Gravitational Wave Detector), suggests this might not be the complete picture of black hole birth. The team behind the research suggests some massive stars go out with a whimper rather than a bang and that these "failed supernovas" can also spawn black holes. The hint of this comes from the over 300 black hole collisions spotted by LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA since the detectors first "heard" ripples in space from these distant events in 2015. "A vast majority of the merging black holes in the universe are about 10 times the mass of our sun," LIGO team member Katerina Chatziioannou, of the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), said in a statement. "Our data are showing that this group of black holes may have a common origin — they may be a distinct subpopulation that failed to go supernova. "These results represent a connection between the gravitational-wave data and underlying astrophysics we are trying to extract." Mass and spin of black holes indicate stars died with a whimper not a bang Currently, there is no hard evidence of failed supernovas, but their existence is well supported theoretically. In fact, scientists think there is a vast population of massive stars out there that imploded rather than exploded, directly collapsing into black holes. And these may be black holes with around ten times the mass of the sun (10 solar masses) found in merging pairs. Chatziioannou led a team that examined gravitational wave data to confirm this concept. To do this, they looked at the distribution of the masses of 257 black hole mergers detected by the LIGO – Virgo – KAGRA network over the past 10 years. This revealed a peak of 10-solar-mass black holes that represented 75% of the entire sample. If this was expected, what the team found that wasn't predicted was a lack of black holes with masses 12 to 16 times the mass of the sun. "We see 10 solar-mass black holes merging all the time," team member Isaac Legred of the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign said. "But why are, say, 14 solar-mass black holes so rare? The gap we see in the distribution of masses indicates there may be a special cocktail of internal physics that goes into forming the abundance of 10 solar-mass black holes." item.title: ULA lost a Vulcan Centaur rocket carrying 40 Amazon satellites 10 minutes after launch — but the failure began just after liftoff
item.description: null The failure of a Vulcan Centaur rocket carrying a full load of internet satellites for Amazon was caused by an anomaly in its first-stage booster, rocket maker United Launch Alliance said today (Nov. 17). That failure — which led to the loss of 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites — was recognized about 10 minutes after liftoff, but the problems began much earlier than that, ULA said in a statement. "While we appear to have lost telemetry and the mission at approximately 10 minutes into flight, early indications are that just after liftoff the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance, resulting in stage separation occurring when the vehicle was low in altitude and below minimal velocity to reach orbit," ULA wrote in today's update . The two-stage Vulcan Centaur is the successor to ULA's workhorse Atlas V rocket, which will retire after just six more flights. Vulcan debuted in January 2024 and now has a total of five launches under its belt. The new rocket has experienced problems on three of those missions. On both its second and fourth flights — which launched in October 2024 and February of this year, respectively — the nozzle of one of Vulcan's strap-on solid rocket boosters (SRBs) fell off about 30 seconds after liftoff. On both occasions, the rocket overcame the problem and successfully delivered its payloads to orbit. However, after the second occurrence, the U.S. Space Force paused national-security launches with Vulcan until ULA addressed the SRB nozzle issue. (The February 2026 flight was a Space Force mission.) That work led to "design and process improvements to the nozzle," ULA said in an Oct. 28 update . And those tweaks apparently worked. "All indications are that the solid rocket booster performance was nominal, following nozzle improvements implemented for this launch," the company wrote in today's update. Vulcan's Centaur V upper stage, which features two RL-10C engines, did its job as well "but was unable to recover from the [booster] performance loss, resulting in loss of mission," ULA added. The Vulcan Centaur lifts off from Florida's Cape Canaveral Space Force Station on Nov. 15, 2026. (Image credit: ULA) Vulcan's first-stage booster is powered by two BE-4 engines, which are built by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin . Today's update did not identify the exact problem with the booster; doing so will require more time, as the investigation has just begun. If that investigation finds a serious issue with the BE-4, there could be broad ripple effects across the American space program. After all, that engine also powers the first stage of Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket, which is a key piece of hardware for NASA's Artemis program of moon exploration. (And New Glenn is currently recovering from a failure of its own — a massive explosion on the test stand that occurred on May 28 .) NASA plans to integrate the Centaur V upper stage into its Space Launch System moon rocket, the vehicle that launches Artemis astronauts

item.title: Entertainment Week Africa officially kicks Off 5th Edition in Lagos | November 17th – 22nd
item.description: Entertainment Week Africa (EWA) , the pan-African platform for the business of creativity, opens its fifth edition in Lagos tomorrow, Wednesday, 18 November. The programme runs until Saturday, 21 November, and brings together creators, executives, investors, policymakers and delegations from more than 18 African countries. This year’s theme, Five Years of Closing the Gap, reflects the purpose EWA was built around: connecting African talent with the capital, markets, skills and audiences it needs to grow. Since its first edition, EWA has welcomed more than 67,800 attendees. The 2025 edition alone recorded 28,683 pass-holders from over eight countries and 50 industries, across 61 sessions, 93 film screenings, 20 music showcases and nine fashion showcases. By day and by night The week runs across two venues. By day, EbonyLife Place on Victoria Island hosts panels, roundtables, workshops, masterclasses, and film screenings. By night, the programme moves to the Livespot Entertarium in Ikate, beginning with Opening Night on 18 November at 6pm, an evening of music, fashion, film, comedy and awards. The Entertarium also houses the week’s experiences, including an exhibition, the EWA Art Floor, a fashion show, comedy, live music, a beauty exhibition and a marketplace. Seven tracks, one market The 2026 programme is organised across seven tracks: Film & TV; Music; Fashion & Beauty; AI & Tech; Live Events & Production; Creative Enterprise; and Art & Animation, which is new this year. Alongside the conference, EWA runs a set of commercial formats designed to move deals forward. They include the EWA Deal Room, the Content and Music Markets, the EWA Capital Desk, the Creators Hub and LABSPOT, EWA’s skills and enterprise development engine. Last year’s Deal Room received more than 178 entries and advanced nine companies to its accelerator, with Future Africa, Catalyst Fund, Consonance Invest and Askya Investment Partners among the participating investors and partners. Between 30 and 40 per cent of this year’s delegates are expected to travel from outside Nigeria, with delegations from Kenya, Rwanda, Ghana, Senegal, Uganda, Tanzania and South Africa among them. The edition will also host the exclusive screening of University of Side Hustle, the first scripted feature film from Livespot Studios, written by Dami Elebe , executive produced by Deola Art Alade. The road to Lagos The fifth edition follows a year in which EWA took its conversation abroad through EWA Creative Connect, its invitation-only convenings. The first was held in Los Angeles during Grammy Week, with executives from Warner Records, Adobe, Amazon and Unilever among the participants. The second took place in London during the Nigeria–UK state visit, with the British Film Institute, Diageo and the Ministry of Trade and Investment in attendance. item.title: On this day in space! Nov. 17, 1967: NASA's Surveyor 6 moon probe makes 1st-ever successful launch and hop from the lunar surface
item.description: null On Nov. 17, 1967, NASA's Surveyor 6 spacecraft made the first liftoff from the lunar surface. Surveyor 6 was one of several robotic lunar missions NASA sent to scout the moon before sending humans there. It took television pictures of the surface and learned about the composition of lunar soil. Then came the big liftoff. First Surveyor 6 launched from the surface and hopped to another position about 8 feet (2 meters) away. Next, Surveyor 6 took pictures of its original landing site. Flight controllers on Earth could see the landing pad prints of Surveyor 6. They also saw an imprint from the rocket exhaust when Surveyor 6 lifted off. Surveyor 6 showed that spacecraft could land on the moon, and lift off again. Less than two years later, humans did the same thing during Apollo 11 . A panorama of the moon from NASA's Surveyor 6 moon lander in November 1967. (Image credit: NASA/GSFC/LROC) Why it mattered NASA's Surveyor 6 spacecraft launched to the moon on Nov. 7, 1967 and made its first landing on the lunar surface on Nov. 10 of that year. It's primary mission was to make a soft landing on the moon in the Sinus Medii of the moon. The probe took nearly 30,000 photos of the moon during its 16 days on the lunar surface, with the lander shutting down due to the onset of lunar night on Nov. 26. Surveyor 6 was the sixth and penultimate moon mission of NASA's Surveyor lunar program, so a lot of what it did (launching and landing on the moon ) had been done before. But a lunar liftoff? That was something new. This Boeing diagram depicts the short launch and hop on the moon by NASA's Surveyor 6 moon lander on Nov. 17, 1967. (Image credit: NASA/GSFC/LROC via Boeing) "On November 17, as an engineering test to see if its rockets could be restarted on the Moon, Surveyor’s engines fired for 2.5 seconds, lifting the spacecraft 12 feet high and moving it 8 feet west of its original landing site, in the first powered liftoff from another celestial body," NASA wrote in a mission overview . The engineering test proved that a spacecraft could land on the moon, and then lift off and take flight once more. That capability was a core requirement for NASA's Apollo astronaut moon landings that followed, since astronauts needed a way to return home after visiting the moon. But there was critical science Surveyor 6 was able to do with the lunar hop. "This maneuver provided excellent views of the surface disturbances produced by the initial landing and the effects of firing rocket engines close to the lunar surface," scientists with the Lunar and Planetary Institute wrote in a summary . "Photography obtained after the hop contributed to the soil mechanics investigation." Surveyor 6 also had a bar magnet on its footpad that allowed scientists to test how magnetic the lunar regolith was at the landing site. Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube .

item.title: Visa Report Identifies Opportunity to Integrate Digital Payments with SMEs Business Operations in Nigeria
item.description: Report identifies next SME digitization opportunity: connecting payments with day-to-day business management. 94% of SMEs surveyed find an all-in-one payment and business solution appealing, yet only 29% currently use one, pointing to untapped demand for tools that connect payments with business management. Integrated payment and business solutions can give financial institutions a more holistic view of SME cash flow and support more tailored financing solutions over time. Small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in Nigeria have largely moved beyond the first stage of digital payment adoption, but a productivity gap remains. According to Visa’s new survey for its Pay and Get Paid 2026 report, most of the SMEs surveyed in Nigeria use digital payments, showing how firmly digital commerce has taken root in the country’s small business economy. However, many SMEs still manage the related financial and operational tasks separately, with only 29% currently using an integrated solution that connects payments with broader business management. The report shows that financial admin and disconnected tools create friction for SMEs, with surveyed businesses citing challenges in tracking outstanding invoices (14%), keeping payroll records organized (19%), and preparing financial reports (16%). These pain points reflect a disconnect between payments and the operational tasks that follow, with some businesses juggling multiple systems to keep their business running. The appetite for a more connected approach is clear. According to the report, 94% of SMEs find an all-in-one payment and business solution appealing, reflecting strong interest in tools that can bring payments and key business operations into one experience. However, adoption has yet to catch up: only 29% of SMEs currently use an integrated payment and business platform. The report points to several perception barriers that may be slowing adoption. Businesses cited that they already have manual processes that work (8%), that an integrated platform may disrupt their current way of working (8%), or that they do not trust relying on a single provider (7%). These findings suggest that broader adoption will depend on helping SMEs better understand how integrated tools can be relevant, accessible, and scalable for businesses at different stages of growth. At the same time, the experience of SMEs already using integrated solutions suggests a strong value case. The report found that Nigerian businesses using an integrated tool or platform report 93% satisfaction, with 88% reporting efficiency gains, including reductions in the time and effort required to manage their business. Beyond efficiency, integrated platforms may also create new opportunities for financial institutions to deepen SME relationships by using richer payments and business-management data to better understand cash flow patterns, support risk assessment, and potentially enable more relevant lending solutions over time. item.title: NASA wants you to 'shine bright' today for Voyager 1's light-day milestone. Here's how
item.description: null As NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft prepares to reach a historic distance from Earth, the agency is inviting people around the world to celebrate by shining a light into the night sky in honor of humanity's farthest-flung spacecraft. The event, called "Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day," will take place after sunset on Tuesday (Nov. 17), the day before Voyager 1 gets one light-day from Earth . And that's a big milestone: One light-day is the distance light travels in a day — about 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers). NASA is encouraging "Shine Bright" participants to create a symbolic wave of golden light around the planet by flashing the spacecraft's three-letter mission call sign, VGR, in Morse code, according to a statement from the space agency. To celebrate the spacecraft, participants can use a flashlight, phone, bike light or other portable light source to send the signal skyward. And don't fret if you're unfamiliar with Morse code : NASA has created an automated flasher that can be opened in a smartphone or tablet browser to display the VGR sequence. The spacecraft’s call sign pattern consists of three quick flashes followed by one long flash for the letter V, two long flashes and one quick flash for G, and one quick flash, one long flash and another quick flash for R. Participants are encouraged to repeat the sequence for about a minute, NASA officials said. The three-letter call sign for NASA's Voyager mission, VGR, spelled out in Morse code. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) NASA also invites people to photograph or record their light signals and share them on social media, tagging the agency's official account, @NASA. The goal is to create a worldwide display of light marking a milestone nearly five decades in the making. The celebration is intended as a symbolic tribute rather than an actual attempt to communicate with Voyager 1 . At a distance of one light-day from Earth, the spacecraft is so far away that even radio signals traveling at the speed of light take approximately 24 hours to reach it. A flashlight or phone signal from Earth, of course, cannot reach the probe; NASA communicates with it using its Deep Space Network of radio dishes. Voyager 1 will get one light-day from Earth on Nov. 18, 2026. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) Launched on Sept. 5, 1977, Voyager 1 has spent nearly 50 years traveling through space and is now the most distant human-made object from Earth. When it reaches the one-light-day milestone, it will have traveled a distance that light itself takes 24 hours to cross. Its twin, Voyager 2 , is expected to reach the same milestone in November 2035. (The two spacecraft took different routes through the solar system.) The public celebration will be followed by another opportunity to learn more about the historic mission.
